707851.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kónsmos, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱónsmos, from *ḱens- (“to announce, put in order”). Related to Latin cēnseō (“to estimate”) and Sanskrit शंसति (śaṃsati, “to commend, praise”).

707836.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kórwā, whence also Mycenaean Greek 𐀒𐀷 (ko-wa). In this word, α (ā) shifted to η (ē) in Attic (see Attic–Ionic vowel shift on Wikipedia) because of the preceding ϝ (w).

707841.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kórwos (“boy”) (whence Mycenaean Greek 𐀒𐀺 (ko-wo)), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱer- (“to grow”); see also Old Armenian սերիմ (serim, “be born”) and սերեմ (serem, “bring forth”), Ancient Greek κόρη (kórē, “girl”) and κορέννυμι…

707871.t: From the old oblique stem, *κραν- (*krān-), of κάρη (kắrē, “Homeric form of κάρα (kắrā, “the head”)”) + -ιον (-ĭon, diminutive suffix).

707883.t: From Proto-Indo-European *krét-os, from *kret- (“strength; intelligence”). Cognates include Sanskrit क्रतु (krátu), Avestan 𐬑𐬭𐬀𐬙𐬎- (xratu-), and Old English heard (“hard”) (whence English hard).

707889.t: Earlier Proto-Hellenic *kréwas, from Proto-Indo-European *kréwh₂s. Cognates include Sanskrit क्रविस् (kravís), Latin cruor (Italian crudo), Proto-Slavic *kry, and Old English hrǣw (English raw).

707879.t: From κράτος (krátos, “power, might”) + -έω (-éō, denominative verbal suffix).

707817.t: From the o-grade κοντ- (kont-) of the root κεντ- (kent-) underlying κεντέω (kentéō, “prick”), κέντρον (kéntron, “centre”). The suffix is -ός (-ós, deverbal adjective and noun suffix).

707829.t: Probably a yod-present formation from a Proto-Indo-European *(s)kop- (“to strike, to beat”) (though there is a chance that the word is a substrate borrowing). Compare Proto-Slavic *skopiti (“to castrate”).

707844.t: According to Beekes, from a Pre-Greek root common to κόρυμβος (kórumbos, “tip of a ship or mountain”) and κόρυς (kórus, “helmet”), based on κορυφ-/κορυμβ- alternation with the aforementioned κόρυμβος (kórumbos).

707880.t: From a zero grade of Proto-Indo-European *ḱerh₂-, whence also κεράννυμι (keránnumi, “to mix”), + -τήρ (-tḗr).

707831.t: From Proto-Indo-European *ḱorh₂k-, from *ḱorh₂- (“crow, raven”). Cognates include Latin corvus, cornix.

707816.t: From an o-grade of Proto-Indo-European *ken- (“dust; ashes”). Cognate with Latin cinis (“cold ashes”), Tocharian B kentse (“dust; rust”), and Sanskrit कण॑ (káṇa).

707845.t: From Proto-Indo-European *ḱorh₂- (“crow, raven”), apparently of imitative origin and with similar formations across multiple Indo-European branches; see Latin cornīx (“crow”) for more.

707868.t: Probably related to κρώζω (krṓzō, “I croak”) and κραυγή (kraugḗ, “cry”)

707807.t: Probably onomatopoeic. Compare βόμβος (bómbos, “humming, buzzing”), κόναβος (kónabos, “din, clash”) and κόμβα (kómba, “shearwater”).

707859.t: From Proto-Hellenic *korsā́, a primary verbal noun from Proto-Indo-European *kers- (“to shave”), an s-extension of *(s)ker- (“to cut”), the same root of κείρω (keírō, “to cut, shear, crop”), κόρση (kórsē, “temple (of forehead)”), and κορμός (kormós, “trunk…

707865.t: Uncertain; Beekes and Furnee take the word as the usual Pre-Greek, while others have narrowed down the language of origin to possibly Semitic or Hurrian.

707895.t: Traditionally considered an old verbal noun from κρεμάννυμι (kremánnumi, “to hang”), however Beekes finds this impossible and leaves the etymology unexplained.

707828.t: From Proto-Indo-European *ḱókʷ-ro-s, thematicized from *ḱókʷr̥ (“excrement”). Cognates include Old Irish cechar (“quagmire, slough, bog”), Sanskrit शकृत् (śakṛt, “dung”), and Lithuanian šiknà (“arse”), ši̇̀kti (“defecate”).

707872.t: Unknown. Traditionally analyzed as an old compound of κάρα (kárā, “head”) (in the form κράσ-), with a faded second member πέδον (pédon, “plain, ground”), for which Sanskrit द्रुपद (drupada, “wooden pillar, post”) is compared.

707824.t: From κοπία (kopĭ́ā, “rest from toil”) + -άω (-ắō), from κόπος (kópos, “beating, suffering, work”) from κόπτω (kóptō, “to strike”).

707896.t: From Proto-Indo-European *kr̥s-neh₂, from *kres- (“spring, fount”). Cognate with Proto-Germanic *hraznō.

707863.t: Of unknown origin; Beekes notes that the full grade of the stem and barytonesis of the word suggest that it was originally a noun and not an adjective, though he leaves the origin open without mentioning any potential comparanda.

707803.t: Not explained with certainty. The word may be taken as "well-tended hair", in opposition of θρίξ (thríx, “hair”), and connected with κομέω (koméō, “to take care of, tend”).

707892.t: Possibly evolved from an original sense of “weak, flaccid”, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱremh₂- (“to hang”).

707843.t: Probably from a Mediterranean Pre-Greek substrate word, as hinted by the suffixes. Traditionally linked to Proto-Indo-European *ḱer- (“head, top, skull, horn”).

707891.t: Altered from earlier κρέσσων (kréssōn), from Proto-Indo-European *kretyōs, from *kret- (whence κρατύς (kratús)). Synchronically, κρατύς (kratús) + *-ϳων (*-jōn).

707842.t: Perhaps related to κόρυς (kórŭs, “helmet”), referring to the thick end of the weapon. According to Beekes, the word is of Pre-Greek origin.

707855.t: Furnée asserts a relation to Latin catīnus (“flat dish”), claiming that the deviation in vowel and formation suggests that they are independent loans from a third party, and adducing κόνδυ (kóndŭ, “cup”) and κονδύλιον (kondŭ́lion), with the observation…

707886.t: Apparently from a Proto-Indo-European *kraw-g- (“to cry”) of imitative origin, similar to κράζω (krázō) and κρώζω (krṓzō).

707870.t: From κεράννυμι (keránnumi, “to mix”) and the suffix -μα (-ma).

707873.t: From Proto-Indo-European *kret-, the root of κρατερός (kraterós).

707897.t: Derived from a nominal base form, like κνημίς (knēmī́s) and χειρίς (kheirī́s), or perhaps this word just took over their ending; the technical meaning suggests a loan.

707835.t: An iterative deverbative verb, lacking a good etymology.

707808.t: Like many words ending in -υ (-ŭ), it is a loanword.

707819.t: From the root of κόπτω (kóptō, “to beat, strike, cut”) + -άζω (-ázō).

707804.t: From Proto-Indo-European *ḱemh₂- (“to exert oneself, get tired”), the same root as κάμνω (kámnō) and κομέω (koméō).
